CHAPTER 2.1 · LEARNING AREA 2 · DECEMBER · JANUARY

Fractions

Half a loaf, a quarter of an hour, three eighths of a pizza, two thirds of the class: you meet parts of a whole every day. In this chapter you learn to write and show parts as fractions, to find fractions on the number line, to work out fractions of quantities and to compare and estimate fractions cleverly.

11 LESSONS4 UNITS1 LOOK AHEAD
WHAT YOU WILL LEARN IN THIS CHAPTER
  • write parts as a fraction and show them on shapes and solids
  • tell proper and improper fractions apart
  • mark fractions on the number line and read them off
  • work out fractions of amounts and quantities: $\tfrac23$ of 24, $\tfrac34$ kg
  • compare fractions without long calculations, for example with one half
CHECK-IN: CAN YOU ALREADY DO THIS?

How many minutes are half an hour?

Half of 60 minutes: 30 minutes.

How many grams are half a kilogram?

$1{,}000 \div 2 = 500$

Calculate: $24 \div 4$

$24 \div 4 = 6$

A quarter of 100 is?

$100 \div 4 = 25$

UNIT 13 LESSONS

1Recognising and showing parts

A pizza is cut into 8 pieces of the same size. Jonas eats 3 pieces. He has eaten three eighths of the pizza. You write $\tfrac38$. A number like this is called a fraction.

Below the fraction line is the denominator: it says into how many equal parts the whole is divided. Above the fraction line is the numerator: it counts how many of these parts are meant. A fraction with the numerator 1, such as $\tfrac13$, is called a unit fraction.

The whole can be a circle, a rectangle, a line segment, a bar of chocolate or a solid made of small cubes. If the numerator is smaller than the denominator, the fraction is less than one whole: a proper fraction. For an improper fraction such as $\tfrac54$ you need more than one whole: one whole and another quarter.

KEY POINT · FRACTIONS

$\tfrac{3}{8}$: numerator 3, denominator 8. The denominator says into how many equal parts the whole is divided. The numerator says how many of them are meant.

Proper fraction: numerator smaller than the denominator, less than 1 whole: $\tfrac38$.   Improper fraction: numerator at least as big as the denominator: $\tfrac44 = 1$, $\tfrac54$ is more than 1.

The same size! Only if all the parts are the same size is each part a quarter, a fifth or an eighth.

How to say them: a half, a third, a quarter, a fifth, …, a tenth, a twentieth, a hundredth.

INTERACTIVE · FRACTIONS AS PICTURES

Set the numerator and the denominator and choose a picture. If the numerator gets bigger than the denominator, a second whole is added.

EXAMPLE 1 · READING OFF A FRACTION

A rectangle is made of 12 squares of the same size. 5 squares are blue. What fraction is blue, and what fraction is not?

The whole has 12 equal parts; 5 of them are blue, the other $12 - 5 = 7$ are not.

Blue: $\tfrac{5}{12}$. Not blue: $\tfrac{7}{12}$. Together $\tfrac{12}{12}$, the whole.

EXAMPLE 2 · DRAWING TWO THIRDS

Draw a strip 6 cm long and colour in $\tfrac23$ of it.

One third is $6\text{ cm} \div 3 = 2\text{ cm}$. Two thirds are twice as long.

Colour in 4 cm of the strip.

EXERCISES

Write as a fraction: a) three quarters   b) five eighths   c) one tenth   d) seven thirds

a) $\tfrac34$   b) $\tfrac58$   c) $\tfrac{1}{10}$   d) $\tfrac73$

Proper or improper fraction? $\tfrac25$, $\tfrac94$, $\tfrac66$, $\tfrac{11}{12}$, $\tfrac72$

Proper: $\tfrac25$ and $\tfrac{11}{12}$. Improper: $\tfrac94$, $\tfrac66 = 1$ and $\tfrac72$.

A big cube is built from 27 small cubes, three layers of $3 \times 3$ cubes each. The top layer is red. What fraction of the small cubes is red?

One layer has 9 cubes, so 9 of 27 are red: $\tfrac{9}{27}$. That is one of three layers of the same size, so $\tfrac13$.

Draw three strips, each 12 cm long. Colour in a) $\tfrac14$   b) $\tfrac23$   c) $\tfrac56$. How long is the coloured part each time?

a) $12 \div 4 = 3$, so 3 cm   b) $12 \div 3 = 4$, $2 \times 4 = 8$, so 8 cm   c) $12 \div 6 = 2$, $5 \times 2 = 10$, so 10 cm

Mia divides a circle into three strips with two parallel lines and colours in the middle strip. She says: “That is a third.” Is she right?

Draw it. Are the three strips the same size?

No. Even if the lines are the same distance apart, the middle strip is bigger than the two pieces at the edge, because the circle is widest in the middle. It is only a third if the three parts are the same size, for example three equal slices of cake.

TEST YOURSELF!

A cake has 12 pieces of the same size; 5 have been eaten. What fraction is still there?

There are still $12 - 5 = 7$ pieces: $\tfrac{7}{12}$.

How many eighths make one whole?

$\tfrac88 = 1$: eight eighths.

How many quarters together make 2 wholes?

One whole has 4 quarters, two wholes have 8 quarters: $\tfrac84 = 2$.

UNIT 22 LESSONS

2Fractions on the number line

The way from the school to the baker’s is 1 km long. After a quarter of the way comes the crossroads, after three quarters the traffic lights. On the number line you divide the stretch from 0 to 1 into 4 equal parts: the crossroads are at $\tfrac14$, the traffic lights at $\tfrac34$.

Fractions are numbers, and every number has its place on the number line. The denominator says into how many equal parts the stretch from 0 to 1 is divided, the numerator how many parts you go to the right. Improper fractions lie to the right of 1: $\tfrac54$ lies a quarter beyond 1.

Sometimes different fractions lie at the same place: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac24$ and $\tfrac48$ are the same number. And natural numbers can be written as fractions: $\tfrac44 = 1$, $\tfrac84 = 2$.

KEY POINT · FRACTIONS ON THE NUMBER LINE

Divide the stretch from 0 to 1 into as many equal parts as the denominator says. Go as many parts to the right as the numerator says.

Improper fractions lie to the right of 1. At the same place lie, for example, $\tfrac12 = \tfrac24 = \tfrac48$.

A clever length: for halves, thirds, quarters and sixths, use 12 cm or 12 squares from 0 to 1. Then everything works out.

One half: if the numerator is exactly half of the denominator, the fraction lies at $\tfrac12$: $\tfrac36$, $\tfrac{5}{10}$, $\tfrac{12}{24}$.

INTERACTIVE · TWO FRACTIONS ON THE NUMBER LINE

Enter two fractions, for example 3/4 and 5/4. The small marks show how each fraction divides the line.

EXAMPLE 3 · READING OFF

The stretch from 0 to 1 is divided into 5 equal parts, and the number line goes up to 2. Which fraction is at the 3rd mark, and which at the 7th mark?

One part is a fifth. At the 3rd mark: $\tfrac35$. At the 7th mark: $\tfrac75$, which lies beyond 1, because $\tfrac55 = 1$.

$\tfrac35$ and $\tfrac75$

EXAMPLE 4 · MARKING FRACTIONS

Mark $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac56$ and $\tfrac32$ on a number line on which the stretch from 0 to 1 is exactly 12 cm long.

One third: $12 \div 3 = 4$ cm. One sixth: 2 cm, five sixths: 10 cm. One half: 6 cm, three halves: 18 cm.

$\tfrac13$ at 4 cm, $\tfrac56$ at 10 cm, $\tfrac32$ at 18 cm

EXERCISES

Draw a number line from 0 to 2, using 8 cm for one whole. Mark $\tfrac14$, $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac78$, $\tfrac54$ and $\tfrac32$ on it.

$\tfrac14$ at 2 cm, $\tfrac12$ at 4 cm, $\tfrac78$ at 7 cm, $\tfrac54$ at 10 cm, $\tfrac32$ at 12 cm.

Which natural numbers are these? $\tfrac63$, $\tfrac{10}{5}$, $\tfrac{12}{4}$, $\tfrac77$

$\tfrac63 = 2$, $\tfrac{10}{5} = 2$, $\tfrac{12}{4} = 3$, $\tfrac77 = 1$

Find three fractions that lie at the same place as $\tfrac12$.

For example $\tfrac24$, $\tfrac36$, $\tfrac{5}{10}$, $\tfrac{50}{100}$: the numerator is always half of the denominator.

Between which natural numbers do $\tfrac72$, $\tfrac94$ and $\tfrac{11}{3}$ lie?

$\tfrac72$: 3 wholes and a half, between 3 and 4.   $\tfrac94$: 2 wholes and a quarter, between 2 and 3.   $\tfrac{11}{3}$: 3 wholes and two thirds, between 3 and 4.

Lena claims: “There is no fraction between $\tfrac14$ and $\tfrac24$, because there is no mark in between.” Is she right?

Divide each quarter into two halves again. What are the new parts called?

No. If you halve each quarter, you get eighths: $\tfrac14 = \tfrac28$ and $\tfrac24 = \tfrac48$. Exactly in between lies $\tfrac38$. With a finer division you can always find more fractions.

TEST YOURSELF!

The stretch from 0 to 1 is divided into 6 equal parts. Which fraction is at the 5th mark?

Five sixths: $\tfrac56$.

Which natural number is $\tfrac{15}{5}$?

Five fifths are one whole, 15 fifths are 3 wholes.

How many thirds fit between 0 and 2?

One whole has 3 thirds, two wholes have 6 thirds: $\tfrac63 = 2$.

UNIT 34 LESSONS

3Fractions of quantities

There are 24 pupils in class 5b. Two thirds of them go by bus. How many is that? One third of 24 is $24 \div 3 = 8$. Two thirds are twice as many: $2 \times 8 = 16$.

To work out a fraction of a quantity, you first divide the whole into as many equal parts as the denominator says. Then you take as many parts as the numerator says.

This also works with quantities such as money, length, mass and time. Often you first convert into a smaller unit: $\tfrac34$ kg is $\tfrac34$ of 1,000 g, so $1{,}000 \div 4 \times 3 = 750$ g. The other way round, you can ask what fraction you have: 450 g of 900 g is half.

KEY POINT · WORKING OUT FRACTIONS OF QUANTITIES

$\tfrac{a}{b}$ of a whole: 1. divide by the denominator, 2. multiply by the numerator.

$\tfrac23$ of 24: $24 \div 3 = 8$, $8 \times 2 = 16$.   $\tfrac34$ of 1 kg: $1{,}000\text{ g} \div 4 = 250\text{ g}$, $3 \times 250\text{ g} = 750\text{ g}$.

Worth remembering: $\tfrac12$ h = 30 min, $\tfrac14$ h = 15 min, $\tfrac34$ h = 45 min, $\tfrac12$ kg = 500 g, $\tfrac14$ kg = 250 g, $\tfrac12$ m = 50 cm.

Backwards: 8 of 24 pupils are $\tfrac{8}{24}$, which is the same as $\tfrac13$.

INTERACTIVE · FRACTIONS IN GROUPS

Set the numerator, the denominator and the whole. The whole is divided into groups of the same size, as many as the denominator says.

EXAMPLE 5 · A DISTANCE

The Berger family cycles 27 km. After $\tfrac23$ of the way they take a break. How far have they cycled by then?

$27\text{ km} \div 3 = 9\text{ km}$, $2 \times 9\text{ km} = 18\text{ km}$.

It is 18 km to the break.

EXAMPLE 6 · WHAT FRACTION?

a) What fraction of 900 g is 450 g?   b) What fraction of an hour is 15 minutes?

a) $450 \times 2 = 900$, so half. b) 15 min goes into 60 min 4 times, so a quarter.

a) $\tfrac12$   b) $\tfrac14$

EXERCISES

Work out: a) $\tfrac14$ of 36   b) $\tfrac35$ of 40   c) $\tfrac56$ of 42   d) $\tfrac78$ of 64

a) 9   b) $40 \div 5 \times 3 = 24$   c) $42 \div 6 \times 5 = 35$   d) $64 \div 8 \times 7 = 56$

Convert: a) $\tfrac34$ h into minutes   b) $\tfrac25$ kg into grams   c) $\tfrac{3}{10}$ m into centimetres   d) $\tfrac23$ of a day into hours

a) 45 min   b) $1{,}000 \div 5 \times 2 = 400$ g   c) $100 \div 10 \times 3 = 30$ cm   d) $24 \div 3 \times 2 = 16$ h

Of the 28 pupils in class 5a, $\tfrac37$ have a pet. How many do not have a pet?

$28 \div 7 = 4$, $3 \times 4 = 12$ have a pet. So $28 - 12 = 16$ do not have one.

What fraction is it? a) 20 min of 1 h   b) 250 g of 1 kg   c) 6 of 30 pupils

a) $\tfrac13$, because 20 min goes into 60 min 3 times   b) $\tfrac14$   c) $\tfrac15$, because 6 goes into 30 5 times

$\tfrac34$ of a footpath is 600 m. How long is the whole path?

How long is one quarter?

Three quarters are 600 m, so one quarter is $600\text{ m} \div 3 = 200\text{ m}$. The whole path is $4 \times 200\text{ m} = 800\text{ m}$ long.

TEST YOURSELF!

How many are $\tfrac23$ of 24 pupils?

$24 \div 3 = 8$, $8 \times 2 = 16$

How many grams are $\tfrac34$ kg?

$1{,}000 \div 4 = 250$, $250 \times 3 = 750$

How many minutes are $\tfrac35$ h?

$60 \div 5 = 12$, $12 \times 3 = 36$

UNIT 42 LESSONS

4Comparing and estimating fractions

Which is more: $\tfrac25$ or $\tfrac34$ of a pizza? You do not have to calculate: $\tfrac25$ is less than half, because 2 is less than half of 5. $\tfrac34$ is more than half. So $\tfrac34$ is more.

Simple reasoning helps you to compare. If two fractions have the same denominator, the pieces are the same size. If they have the same numerator, you take the same number of pieces, and smaller denominators mean bigger pieces. Often it helps to compare with $\tfrac12$ or with 1.

And sometimes you look at what is missing to make a whole: for $\tfrac78$ an eighth is missing, for $\tfrac56$ a sixth. An eighth is less, so $\tfrac78$ is bigger.

KEY POINT · COMPARING FRACTIONS

Same denominator: the bigger numerator wins: $\tfrac58 > \tfrac38$.

Same numerator: the smaller denominator wins, because its pieces are bigger: $\tfrac25 > \tfrac27$.

Comparing with one half: $\tfrac25 < \tfrac12 < \tfrac34$.

Exactly one half: if the numerator is half of the denominator, the fraction is $\tfrac12$: $\tfrac36$, $\tfrac48$.

Estimating: 9 of 28 is about $\tfrac13$, because 9 of 27 would be exactly one third.

INTERACTIVE · WHICH FRACTION IS BIGGER?

Set two fractions. The dashed line marks one half. Below it says how you can decide without calculating.

EXAMPLE 7 · ORDERING

Put in order from smallest to biggest: $\tfrac38$, $\tfrac58$, $\tfrac18$, $\tfrac88$.

They all have the denominator 8. So the numerators decide: 1, 3, 5, 8.

$\tfrac18 < \tfrac38 < \tfrac58 < \tfrac88 = 1$

EXAMPLE 8 · WHAT IS MISSING?

Which is more: $\tfrac78$ or $\tfrac56$ of a bar of chocolate?

For $\tfrac78$ an eighth of the bar is missing, for $\tfrac56$ a sixth. Eighths are smaller than sixths, so less is missing for $\tfrac78$.

$\tfrac78 > \tfrac56$

EXERCISES

Put in $<$, $>$ or $=$: a) $\tfrac49 \;☐\; \tfrac79$   b) $\tfrac35 \;☐\; \tfrac38$   c) $\tfrac12 \;☐\; \tfrac{5}{10}$   d) $\tfrac27 \;☐\; \tfrac23$

a) $<$   b) $>$   c) $=$   d) $<$

More than, less than or exactly one half? $\tfrac38$, $\tfrac59$, $\tfrac48$, $\tfrac{6}{11}$, $\tfrac{7}{15}$

$\tfrac38$ less, $\tfrac59$ more, $\tfrac48$ exactly, $\tfrac{6}{11}$ more (6 is more than half of 11), $\tfrac{7}{15}$ less.

Compare with one half: a) $\tfrac25$ and $\tfrac47$   b) $\tfrac{5}{12}$ and $\tfrac35$

a) $\tfrac25 < \tfrac12 < \tfrac47$, so $\tfrac47$ is bigger.   b) $\tfrac{5}{12} < \tfrac12 < \tfrac35$, so $\tfrac35$ is bigger.

Put in order from smallest to biggest and give reasons: $\tfrac23$, $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac34$, $\tfrac14$, $\tfrac12$

$\tfrac14 < \tfrac13$ (same numerator) $< \tfrac12 <$ $\tfrac23 < \tfrac34$ (for $\tfrac23$ a third is missing, for $\tfrac34$ only a quarter).

Estimate the fraction with a simple fraction: a) 49 of 100 raffle tickets are blanks.   b) 26 of 79 people come by bike.   c) 11 of 45 games won.

a) about $\tfrac12$   b) about $\tfrac13$, because 26 of 78 would be exactly one third   c) about $\tfrac14$, because 11 of 44 would be exactly one quarter

TEST YOURSELF!

Which fraction is bigger?

Same numerator: fifths are bigger than eighths, so $\tfrac35$ is bigger.

How many fractions with the denominator 10 and a numerator greater than 0 are less than one half?

$\tfrac{1}{10}$, $\tfrac{2}{10}$, $\tfrac{3}{10}$, $\tfrac{4}{10}$: four of them. $\tfrac{5}{10}$ is exactly one half.

Which numerator makes $\tfrac{\square}{14}$ exactly one half?

Half of 14 is 7: $\tfrac{7}{14} = \tfrac12$.

REVIEW · DEEPEN · CONNECT

Time: How many minutes are a) $\tfrac16$ h   b) $\tfrac{5}{12}$ h   c) $1\tfrac12$ h?

a) 10 min   b) $60 \div 12 \times 5 = 25$ min   c) 90 min

Pocket money: Paul gets €24 pocket money a month. He saves $\tfrac38$ of it and spends $\tfrac14$ on the cinema. How much money does he have left for other things?

Saving: $24 \div 8 \times 3 = 9$, so €9. Cinema: $24 \div 4 = 6$, so €6. Left over: $24 - 9 - 6 = 9$, so €9.

Survey: In class 5c (25 people), 10 come on foot, 5 by bike and the rest by bus. Write each share as a fraction. Which fraction is more than one half?

On foot $\tfrac{10}{25}$, by bike $\tfrac{5}{25}$, by bus $\tfrac{10}{25}$. None of them is more than one half, because 10 is less than half of 25.

How much is the whole? Lina has already read $\tfrac25$ of her book, that is 120 pages. How many pages does the book have, and how many are still to go?

Two fifths are 120 pages, so one fifth is 60 pages. The book has $5 \times 60 = 300$ pages, and $300 - 120 = 180$ pages are still to go.

EXCURSIONHISTORY

Fractions in ancient Egypt

One of the oldest maths books in the world is kept today in the British Museum in London: the Rhind Papyrus. A scribe called Ahmose copied it around 1550 BC. It contains more than eighty problems with which scribes learned to calculate, for example how to share out loaves of bread fairly.

The Egyptians wrote fractions almost only as unit fractions, that is with the numerator 1: $\tfrac12$, $\tfrac13$, $\tfrac14$, … They made other fractions up from different unit fractions. Instead of $\tfrac34$ they wrote “$\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac14$”. Right at the beginning of the papyrus there is a big table of such splittings, for example $\tfrac{2}{15} = \tfrac{1}{10} + \tfrac{1}{30}$. Only for $\tfrac23$ did they have a symbol of its own.

Try it yourself: Use a strip of 12 squares to show that $\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac14$ together make $\tfrac34$. How would an Egyptian scribe write $\tfrac{7}{12}$?

$\tfrac12$ is 6 squares, $\tfrac14$ is 3 squares, together 9 of 12 squares, so $\tfrac{9}{12} = \tfrac34$. $\tfrac{7}{12}$ is 7 squares: 6 squares ($\tfrac12$) and 1 square ($\tfrac{1}{12}$). So “$\tfrac12$ and $\tfrac{1}{12}$”.

Source: British Museum, London, object EA 10057 (“Rhind Mathematical Papyrus”), around 1550 BC, scribe Ahmose; collection page britishmuseum.org/collection/object/Y_EA10057.

LOOKING BACKTHE ESSENTIALS AT A GLANCE

FRACTIONS

Denominator: into how many equal parts; numerator: how many of them

$\tfrac38$: 3 of 8 equal pieces

PROPER AND IMPROPER

Proper: less than 1 whole; improper: numerator at least as big as the denominator

$\tfrac34 < 1$; $\tfrac44 = 1$; $\tfrac54 > 1$

NUMBER LINE

0 to 1 in as many parts as the denominator, as many steps to the right as the numerator

$\tfrac12 = \tfrac24 = \tfrac48$ lie at the same place

FRACTIONS OF QUANTITIES

Divide by the denominator, multiply by the numerator

$\tfrac23$ of 24: $24 \div 3 \times 2 = 16$

COMPARING

Same denominator, same numerator, one half, what is missing to make a whole

$\tfrac25 < \tfrac12 < \tfrac34$; $\tfrac78 > \tfrac56$

TESTTWO ROUNDS · INSTANT FEEDBACK
ROUND 1 · WITHOUT A CALCULATOR

A pizza has 8 pieces. 3 pieces have been eaten. What fraction is left?

$8 - 3 = 5$ pieces: $\tfrac58$

Work out $\tfrac56$ of 36.

$36 \div 6 = 6$, $6 \times 5 = 30$

How many grams are $\tfrac14$ kg?

$1{,}000 \div 4 = 250$

ROUND 2 · THINKING

Which fraction is bigger?

For $\tfrac{9}{10}$ a tenth is missing, for $\tfrac{11}{12}$ only a twelfth. So $\tfrac{11}{12}$ is bigger.

$\tfrac{3}{5}$ of a year group are 27 people. How many are there altogether?

One fifth: $27 \div 3 = 9$. Altogether $5 \times 9 = 45$.

Which fraction with the denominator 4 lies between 1 and 2 on the number line and closest to 2?

Between $\tfrac44 = 1$ and $\tfrac84 = 2$ lie $\tfrac54$, $\tfrac64$, $\tfrac74$. Closest to 2: $\tfrac74$.
